title: Trembling and astonishment (Mark 16:1–8)
hook: the women find the tomb empty; the oldest copies end with them fleeing, afraid

segments.voice: Yesterday, a council member who dared to ask for the body, and your line was he went in boldly. Did you do the kindness that made you nervous? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

The Sabbath is over. Very early on Sunday morning, as the sun is coming up, three women walk to the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They've bought spices to anoint his body, the last thing they can do for him. And on the way they're worried about something very practical. Who will roll away the stone for us? It's huge. They'd watched it go in. Then they look up. The stone is already rolled back.
screen: `VERY EARLY, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL AWAY THE STONE?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: They go into the tomb, and sitting on the right side is a young man in a long white robe. They are terrified. And he says, in the King James Bible: "Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." Then he gives them a message: go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said. And Peter. Of all the names to single out, it's the one who denied him three times by the fire. Then comes the last verse of Mark in the oldest copies we have: "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid." That's it. No appearance of the risen Jesus. No reunion. Just women running from an empty tomb, shaking. In Greek, the end of the sentence is literally, they were afraid, for. It ends on a small word, gar, like a sentence cut off mid-breath. Scholars have argued about this for centuries. Maybe the last page was lost. Maybe Mark meant to stop here. If he did, the ending is a kind of invitation: the story isn't finished; it hands the next step to whoever is reading. And we know the women didn't stay silent forever, or there'd be no story to read. The trembling and astonishment are the right response. Not calm, not neat: awe. In Greek, trembling is tromos, and astonishment is ekstasis, which gives English the word ecstasy. Something so big it takes you outside yourself.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN A WHITE ROBE.` · `TELL HIS DISCIPLES, AND PETER.` · `THEY WERE AFRAID, FOR.` · `TROMOS AND EKSTASIS.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with an ending that's also a beginning. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that ended: a job, a friendship, a season, a home. Let yourself feel what the women felt on that walk: the heaviness, the practical worries, who will roll away the stone. Then ask gently: what began after that ending, even if you didn't see it at the time? You don't need a neat answer. Just notice. If you pray, you can hold that ending before God. The bell holds the time.
Trembling and astonishment. What seized the women at the empty tomb, in the last verse of Mark's oldest copies: tromos and ekstasis.
Your line: he goes before you. Today, walk into one place you're dreading, and notice what's already been done before you get there. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection every Easter and every Sunday; many churches hold sunrise services on Easter morning, and Orthodox Christians greet each other with Christ is risen, answered, he is risen indeed.

fork.setup: you've found the stone rolled back and a young man tells you: he is risen, go and tell. what do the women do, in Mark's oldest ending?
options: run and tell everyone at once.
flee, trembling, and say nothing, for they were afraid.
stay and wait at the tomb.
fork.reveal: they fled, trembling and astonished, and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. that's where the oldest copies end.

original.note: Greek: astonishment, being beside yourself. Mark 16:8. English ecstasy comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mark ends with a happy reunion.
what it means: the oldest copies end with the women fleeing an empty tomb, trembling and afraid.
what a scholar hears: the last Greek word is gar, for; scholars still debate whether Mark meant to stop there or the ending was lost.

sources.quoted: Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.
And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.

notes: The oldest complete manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, 4th century) end at 16:8. Confirm 'oldest copies'.
Mark 16:8 uses 'tromos kai ekstasis' ('trembling and astonishment'); KJV renders 'they trembled and were amazed'. The title follows the older rendering; confirm.
The debate (intended ending vs. lost ending) is presented without taking sides.
Tomorrow's day covers the longer ending (16:9–20); this day doesn't teach it.
